# 01 Setup your environment

Run the common setup script and synchronize the local project with
GitHub.

```{r}
# Run the setup script containing package restoration, helper functions, etc.
source(here::here("scripts", "01-setup.r"))

# Pull changes from the online repository into this local project folder.
# This is especially important when collaborating on the same project.
system2("git", c("-C", here::here(), "pull"))

# show which package namespaces are loaded to memory with library()
search()
```

# 02 Variables, vectors, and operators

Variables are named objects used to store values.

```{r}
# Create a variable and assign it the value 32 and print it

```

The equals sign `=` can also be used for assignment, but `<-` is
conventional in R.

## Logical comparison operators

```{r}
# compare different logical comparison operators
class_size == 32 # is class_size equal to 32? Returns TRUE or FALSE
class_size != 35 # is class_size different from 35?
class_size > 20 # is class_size greater than 20?
class_size < 20 # is class_size less than 20?
class_size >= 28 # is class_size greater than or equal to 28?
class_size <= 28 # is class_size less than or equal to 28?
```

# 03 Data frames and tibbles

Data frames organize variables as columns and observations as rows.
A data frame is a table-like object. Each column is a vector and
different columns can have different data types. A data frame is
also a special type of list in which the columns have the same
length, allowing them to form rows.

```{r}

```

## Selecting and filtering with dplyr

The pipe operator `|>` passes the result on the left to the function
on the right, allowing a sequence of operations on a data frame or
tibble.

```{r}
# select and filter rows and columns from the dataframe that you created


```

## Tibbles

A tibble is a modern version of a data frame used by the tidyverse.
Its print method displays variable types and limits the output to
rows and columns that fit conveniently on screen.

# 05 Dates and time

Dates written between quotation marks start as character strings.
The lubridate package provides functions for converting them into
date/time objects.

```{r}
# A date written as text is still a character object
# assign a data to a variable
date_var <- "2023-01-12"
class(date_var)

# But arithmetic does not work as date arithmetic while the value is character.


# Convert year-month-day text into a Date object and inspect it

# Date objects support date arithmetic - check it


```

# 07 Methods of a function

A generic function can behave differently for different classes of
objects. These class-specific implementations are called methods.
`summary()` is a generic function with methods for many classes of
objects.

```{r}
# Create a numeric vector.


# The numeric vector has class "numeric".
# apply the summary function to that vector

# Apply summary() to an object of class "lm".


```

## Inspecting methods

```{r}
# methods() lists the available methods for a generic function, try it on the summary function


```

So R examines the class of an object and dispatches the appropriate
method. For a numeric vector, `summary()` falls back to
`summary.default()`. For an `lm` object, it uses `summary.lm()`.

```{r}
# apply the summary function to the vector object and the model1 object explicitly with the method


```
